target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove major scheduling barriers and make voting easier for more people.
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably remove the work barrier because private employers are not required to give paid holidays or close, so many low-wage retail, food service, and gig workers would still have to work or lose pay.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is a good standalone solution for voting access.
objection: Research and practical experience suggest that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with reforms that directly guarantee time and ease of voting, such as employer time-to-vote rules, expanded early/absentee voting, and automatic voter registration.

target: AG2’s objection that a federal holiday does not guarantee paid time off for private workers and therefore should be opposed.
objection: Even if a holiday alone does not guarantee paid leave, it still reduces practical obstacles, makes planning easier, and can be paired with employer-protection rules; therefore the lack of guaranteed paid leave does not justify opposing the holiday in principle.

target: AG2’s claim that an Election Day holiday would not meaningfully help because private workers could still face access barriers.
objection: A national holiday is still valuable because it changes more than time off: it gives employers and communities a predictable day to plan around voting, reduces day-to-day friction, and helps voters coordinate transportation, childcare, and school-related constraints.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday broadly reduces scheduling barriers and can be paired with employer protections.
objection: The central equity problem remains: without a legal requirement for private employers to provide paid time off or close, low-wage workers at restaurants, retail, hospitals, and other service jobs may still face the same conflict between voting and losing pay.

target: AG1’s suggestion that the holiday should be adopted now and complemented later with employer protections.
objection: If the proposal must be paired with enforceable employer time-to-vote rules to work, then the holiday itself is doing little causal work and adds unnecessary cost and political complexity, while risking passage without the stronger protections.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday changes schedules and logistics broadly enough to help private-sector workers.
objection: For the low-income workforce most constrained by schedules, a holiday may mainly change who can vote rather than making voting easier for everyone; flexible office workers benefit more, so the policy could widen turnout gaps instead of reliably increasing turnout.

target: AG1’s idea that pairing the holiday with employer rules makes the holiday worthwhile.
objection: If enforceable employer time-to-vote requirements are added, then those employer protections—not the holiday—are doing the real work, making the holiday largely redundant and an added political step that could distract from stronger reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday still reduces scheduling friction even in the private sector.
objection: Private-sector workplaces that operate on holidays, such as retail, food service, hospitals, and logistics, still need coverage and often schedule low-wage workers because it is a holiday, so the policy may fail to reduce the main barrier for the most constrained voters and can mainly benefit more flexible workers.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday independently helps private-sector workers and adds value even if paired with other reforms.
objection: If a holiday is combined with enforceable private-employer voting-time rules, the calendar holiday is largely redundant because the enforceable rule—not the holiday—creates the access benefit, while the holiday effort could crowd out more direct reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday changes schedules and logistics across sectors in a way that helps many workers vote.
objection: Holiday staffing patterns in private-sector jobs can still require coverage and may even schedule shift workers because it is a holiday, so the policy may not reduce barriers for the workers most constrained by time and pay.

target: AG1’s broader case that a national Election Day holiday is a strong turnout reform.
objection: The evidence is weak for a holiday on its own: research suggests an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with reforms that directly expand voting time and access.
